planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Arctic Frost was bred for exceptional cold hardiness among satsuma mandarins, allowing gardeners in the cooler parts of zone 8 to grow sweet, seedless, easy-peel citrus that would otherwise require zone 9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting in the warmest available microclimate for the first few winters. Arctic Frost is a satsuma mandarin selection bred for improved cold hardiness beyond standard satsuma cultivars, allowing mature trees to tolerate brief drops into the low 20s or upper teens Fahrenheit with only minor wood damage, when standard citrus of similar fruit quality would be killed to the ground. Fruit is sweet, low-acid, essentially seedless, and easy to peel, with the loose, glossy rind typical of satsumas, ripening in fall to early winter. Young trees need cold protection for the first two to three winters until established, but mature wood is notably tougher than most edible citrus. Like other satsumas, it is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, and it tends to bear well even as a young tree. Protect the trunk and graft union with mulch or wrap in the coldest years, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization in late summer, which can push tender new growth that is more vulnerable to an early freeze.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus for the Southeast
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Citrus for the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cold-Hardy Satsuma Selection

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eustis is the original and most widely grown limequat, a cross of Key lime and kumquat developed in Florida in 1909, combining true lime flavor with cold hardiness well beyond that of any true lime.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a lime-flavored citrus, tolerating temperatures that would kill true Key lime and Persian lime trees outright. Eustis limequat was developed in Eustis, Florida, in 1909 by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle as a cross between Key lime and kumquat, aiming to combine the tart, aromatic lime flavor with the cold hardiness of kumquat, one of the toughest edible citrus species. The resulting small, oval, yellow-gold fruit has a genuinely lime-like tart flavor along with an edible, sweet-tart rind in the kumquat tradition, making the whole fruit usable — sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved in marmalade — without peeling. The compact tree bears prolifically and tolerates cold that would damage or kill a true lime, making it one of the few practical ways to grow lime-flavored citrus in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 outside the true lime-growing range. Protect young trees through their first few winters; mature wood handles cold considerably better. Harvest fruit once it colors up gold, and use promptly, as limequats do not store as long as some other citrus.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Limequat Varieties
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cold-Hardy Citrus for the Home Garden

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Morton is a cold-hardy citrange, a hybrid of trifoliate orange and sweet orange, valued for tart, orange-flavored fruit on a tree that tolerates significantly colder winters than any true orange.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for citrus, with mature wood able to withstand temperatures well below what standard sweet orange trees survive, thanks to trifoliate orange parentage. Morton citrange is a hybrid between trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) and sweet orange, bred primarily to extend cold-hardy citrus growing further north than standard oranges allow. The fruit is tart, seedy, and more acidic than a true sweet orange, generally used for juice, marmalade, or as an ade rather than fresh eating out of hand, though well-ripened fruit mellows considerably. Trees show the trifoliate parent's deciduous or semi-deciduous habit in colder winters and small, three-part leaves, along with light thorns typical of trifoliate hybrids. Because of its unusual hardiness, Morton citrange has been of particular interest to cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing the edible citrus range into zone 6-7, well beyond where standard citrus survives. Protect young trees for the first few winters; established trees are considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored for the best balance of sweetness and acidity.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Citrange Breeding
University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus for the Southeast
North Carolina State Extension — Trifoliate Orange Hybrids

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Titan is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release known for producing the largest berries of any commercial rabbiteye cultivar, on vigorous, upright, productive bushes. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Titan is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry celebrated for producing exceptionally large berries, among the biggest of any rabbiteye cultivar available, with good firmness and a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor that makes for an impressive fresh-eating harvest. The vigorous, upright bushes are productive and ripen mid-to-late in the rabbiteye season, extending the harvest window when paired with earlier cultivars like Alapaha or Premier. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Titan requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Titan Rabbiteye Blueberry Release
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Vaccinium Cultivar Development

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Krewer is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening late in the season, extending the fresh blueberry harvest window well past most other Southern cultivars. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Krewer is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh Southern blueberry harvest into midsummer after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, a valuable trait for home gardeners and market growers wanting to spread out the harvest season. The vigorous, productive bushes bear medium to large berries with good flavor and firmness. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Krewer requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other, choosing early- and mid-season partners to spread bloom timing and further extend the overall harvest. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Krewer Rabbiteye Blueberry Release
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Vaccinium Cultivar Development
